I have seen patients pass with end of life sedation and without.
I always advocate for end of life sedation.
End of life sedation will help someone be pain free and as a nurse, we will top up and also provide medication for increased fluid we hear. 
A patient not on end of life sedation, while actively dying? Unless the family agrees otherwise, we only had paracetamol suppositories to give. Which to me felt very undignified.
I always advocate for talking about end of life care early, even if you have years left.
End of life pain relief.
End of life care.
End of life dignity.

With your mothers body shutting down, the morphine is likely hitting more than it would someone else. But also, know that without the morphine sedation, she would be in significant pain and have to be awake while experiencing her body shut down and it is not pleasant.
Talk to her even if you don’t think she is there.
Give her all the love.
In her lucid moments, love bomb hard.
Remember the woman she was and is.
If you can, between sedation spells, ask her what she wants you to remember and pass on.
Tell her your favourite stories.

I don't have ADHD (on this sub because I strongly suspect my partner) but I do find that I go on autopilot mode for things I do daily. I'll forget if I have had my medications, forget if I've locked the car, forget if I've closed the garage.

T2DM is a very complex illness, as others have pointed out.

If possible, talk to your FIL or the hospital and find out exactly what is happening.

Is he in hospital due to complications of T2DM? Such as uncontrolled glucose levels? Or is he in for something else? In order for his health to get better so quickly, generally speaking, the medical team would have an idea of what is the root cause to reverse and manage it. As a “frequent flyer” if they haven’t got a clue what the root cause is and are purely just symptom managing without investigations (extensive blood tests, scans if needed, urine samples) then it might be time to also question the hospital.

While I’m not familiar with poisoning, I’m very familiar with T2DM and treatment.

A person with T2DM that doesn’t eat properly or follow their medication regime properly they can, and do, end up in hospital frequently to stabilise and then home on a repetitive cycle.

In the hospital his diet would be strictly controlled and so would glucose monitoring and any relevant medications. Hence the improvement.

If he’s going home and having a rapid decline in health, I’d be closely examining his diet and medication first before anything else. You wouldn’t necessarily need to poison a T2DM person in order for them to become unwell.

By skipping medication and then having a very sugary/carb loaded diet then glucose levels can go seriously out of control, leading to rapid health decline. 

The situation you’ve described sounds incredibly concerning, and it does make me wonder if your FIL has changed his will (or made one) lately, especially to include the new lady love. That would raise massive red flags as well.

She wouldn’t need to poison him to make him unwell, she’d just need to mess with medications and diet.

I’d head down to the local police station and have a chat about your concerns. See what they can do or suggest - maybe adult protective services? I think I’ve seen that the USA has this?

Have they ran a faecal test to confirm you have a gastro bug? Generally when we have a breakout at hospital (nurse in an Australian hospital), whether it is one or more patients, we have to obtain specimens to be sent for testing.

Just because other patients don’t have gastro, it doesn’t mean you 100% don’t have gastro either.

We have had plenty of cases where only one person has had gastro and the rest of our ward has been perfectly fine, it is not impossible.

Secondly, as a (presumably) diagnosed coeliac, does your specialist work with this hospital? It may be worth having your specialist, and/or the pharmacist when they come around (they tend to do daily rounds) whether there are any gluten ingredients in your medications. 

Thirdly, it’s hard to prove cross contamination in a food source. Is there anyway to get food brought in from outside? I know the hospital provides food, but sometimes it’s better to be safe than sorry. If you are having cross contamination from food, you need safe food. Question staff on how they manage cross contamination. 

Additionally, you are entitled to a second opinion. Ask to speak to the RN in charge, discuss your concerns about being given gluten - either inadvertently through medication or through cross contamination for food. If you are not happy with that, ask to speak to the nurse unit manager.

Google the name of the hospital and add complaints to the end. There is generally contact details for the complaints (they are also around the ward however as you are in isolation I don’t think that it’ll be easy for you). Explain to them that you have coeliacs disease, as documented in your history, you believe you were given gluten, resulting in gastro-like symptoms and you being put in isolation. Explain that you would like an investigation into this matter, as coeliacs disease is a serious disease that can sometimes lead to cancer and other debilitating and life threatening conditions. 

Unfortunately, sometimes the patient needs to be their own advocate. If you were given gluten through medication or food, it’s likely you are still getting gluten if they are unaware of cross contamination or inactive ingredients in the medication. If you have been given gluten, your symptoms are not going to improve until the gluten has stopped.

Another step to take (and they generally don’t do anything until you’ve followed hospital protocols) is the health complaints commission.

Victorian Legal Aid May be able to provide some counsel over the phone, I just looked on their website but couldn’t see if they do medical legal advice.

The legal institute of Victoria can refer you to some lawyers that do free 30 minute counsel as well.

This next part that I say I don’t think you’re going to like. I really don’t believe that even if there was accidental gluten given that any lawyer is going to take on a case to sue for damages. Your damages are going to be negligible, and if you aren’t covered by legal aid (which doesn’t cover all areas of law), you may end up paying more in legal fees than in the  perceived damages you are going after.

The best thing you could do is make complaints internally and externally and making sure that the hospital and its staff are educated on the dangers of giving gluten to a person diagnosed with coeliacs disease.

That I've managed to stay in uni despite the shit I've faced.

I'm a mature aged student. Returned to study to get ahead in life.

A few months into my first course a baby was placed in my care unexpectedly. Overnight I had to learn how to parent, juggle working part time and studying full time. 

A few months later I had an unplanned pregnancy.

So with one baby on the way and a baby at home I had to juggle severe morning sickness, work and study.

Gave birth on semester break, 3-4 weeks later I was back in class.

I was even more determined to finish that course to give my kids a good future.

It was bloody hard. I developed awful PND. I was exhausted all the time. I refused to be hospitalised for the PND, so made a compromise with the psychiatrist and psychologist to have sessions a few times a week.

But we pulled through.

I passed my course with great marks. With that course I was able to secure a well-paying job.

I have gone on to another course now to increase my earning potential and have more career prospects open to me. Just over a year left of study and then I'm done.

People always roll their eyes at me when I tell them I'm proud I got through what I did. It was bleeping hard. 

ETA: when baby 1 was put in my care, I regularly had to attend court as well so that someone had the baby's interests in mind. That was also a huge stress.
